questions.q: A portfolio has a 1-day 99% VaR of $4.66 million. What does this mean?
options: The portfolio can never lose more than $4.66 million in a day
A one-day loss exceeding $4.66 million is expected on no more than 1% of trading days
The portfolio will lose exactly $4.66 million every 100 days
99% of the portfolio's value is at risk of being lost
questions.explain: VaR at a given confidence level and horizon states the loss threshold that is not expected to be exceeded more often than the stated probability — it is not a hard cap and not a guaranteed loss amount.

questions.q: Which VaR estimation method assumes portfolio returns follow a normal distribution?
options: Historical simulation
Monte Carlo simulation
Parametric (variance-covariance) VaR
Reverse stress testing
questions.explain: Parametric VaR computes VaR directly from the mean and standard deviation of returns under a normality assumption, using VaR = -(mean - z times standard deviation).

questions.q: Why is Value at Risk described as 'tail-blind'?
options: It ignores the first 99% of the return distribution entirely
It cannot be calculated for portfolios with derivatives
It marks a loss threshold but gives no information about how severe losses are beyond that threshold
It only applies to equity portfolios, not bonds
questions.explain: VaR reports a cutoff point. Two portfolios can share the same VaR while differing enormously in how bad their losses get past that cutoff — VaR alone cannot distinguish them.

questions.q: What does it mean for a risk measure to lack 'sub-additivity', a property VaR does not generally guarantee?
options: It cannot be computed using subtraction
The risk of a combined portfolio can exceed the sum of the risks of its individual pieces
It always underestimates risk for single-asset portfolios
It can only be applied to portfolios with fewer than two assets
questions.explain: A sub-additive risk measure guarantees that combining positions never increases total measured risk beyond the sum of the parts. VaR does not guarantee this in general, which can distort diversification and capital-allocation decisions.

questions.q: How does Expected Shortfall (Conditional VaR) differ from VaR itself?
options: Expected Shortfall is simply VaR measured over a longer time horizon
Expected Shortfall reports the average loss given that the loss exceeds the VaR threshold, rather than just the threshold itself
Expected Shortfall only applies to fixed income portfolios
Expected Shortfall and VaR are two names for the exact same calculation
questions.explain: Expected Shortfall averages the losses in the tail beyond the VaR cutoff, directly addressing VaR's tail-blindness, and is a coherent (sub-additive) risk measure — part of why Basel's FRTB rules shifted trading-book capital requirements toward it.
